title: Life of a Packet
summary: The complete end-to-end journey of a packet: ARP, encapsulation, de-encapsulation, and re-encapsulation at every hop from source to destination.

content.body:
This lesson ties together everything from previous lessons — ARP, encapsulation, de-encapsulation, and routing — by following one packet from PC1 (192.168.1.0/24) to PC4 (192.168.4.0/24) across three routers.

Each network device interface has its own **MAC address**. For this example we use short MACs:

| Device | Interface | MAC |
|---|---|---|
| PC1 | eth0 | 1111 |
| R1 | G0/2 (to PC1's LAN) | AAAA |
| R1 | G0/0 (to R2) | BBBB |
| R2 | G0/0 (to R1) | CCCC |
| R2 | G0/1 (to R4) | DDDD |
| R4 | G0/1 (to R2) | EEEE |
| R4 | G0/2 (to PC4's LAN) | FFFE |
| PC4 | eth0 | 4444 |

sections.title: Step 1: PC1 finds its default gateway with ARP

content.body:
PC1 wants to send to 192.168.4.1, which is in a **different network**, so it must send the packet to its **default gateway** (R1, 192.168.1.254). But PC1 doesn't know R1's MAC address, so it sends an **ARP request**:

- Source IP = 192.168.1.1 (PC1), destination IP = 192.168.1.254 (R1).
- Destination MAC = **broadcast** (all Fs), source MAC = 1111.

SW1 floods the broadcast and learns PC1's MAC on its G0/1 port. R1 sees the destination IP is its own and replies with a **unicast ARP reply**: "I am 192.168.1.254, my MAC is AAAA." SW1 learns R1's MAC from that reply. PC1 now knows R1's MAC.

steps.narration: PC1 sends an ARP request (broadcast) to learn its default gateway's MAC address.
R1 replies with a unicast ARP reply: 'My MAC is AAAA.' PC1 now knows R1's G0/2 MAC.
PC1 encapsulates the packet (still destined for 192.168.4.1) in a frame with destination MAC AAAA and sends it to R1.

content.body:
R1 receives the frame and **de-encapsulates** it — removes the Ethernet header and trailer to reveal the packet. The packet is unchanged: source 192.168.1.1, destination 192.168.4.1.

R1 looks up 192.168.4.1 in its routing table. The most specific match is a static route to 192.168.4.0/24 with next-hop **192.168.12.2 (R2)**. R1 doesn't know R2's MAC, so it ARPs: "Who is 192.168.12.2?" R2 replies with its MAC (CCCC). R1 **re-encapsulates** the packet in a new frame — source MAC BBBB, destination MAC CCCC — and sends it out G0/0.

sections.title: R2 to R4, and R4 to PC4

content.body:
**R2** de-encapsulates, looks up 192.168.4.1, and finds a route with next-hop 192.168.24.4 (R4). It ARPs for R4's MAC (EEEE), then re-encapsulates: source MAC DDDD, destination MAC EEEE.

**R4** de-encapsulates and finds 192.168.4.0/24 is **directly connected** on G0/2. It ARPs for PC4's MAC (4444), then re-encapsulates: source MAC FFFE, destination MAC 4444 — and delivers the frame to PC4.

At every hop the **IP addresses never change** (source 192.168.1.1, destination 192.168.4.1), but the **MAC addresses change at every router**, because each hop re-encapsulates the same packet in a new frame.

steps.narration: PC1 → R1: source MAC 1111, destination MAC AAAA.
R1 → R2: source MAC BBBB, destination MAC CCCC.
R2 → R4: source MAC DDDD, destination MAC EEEE.
R4 → PC4: source MAC FFFE, destination MAC 4444. The packet arrives.
PC4 replies. Now that all devices have learned each other's MACs via ARP, no more ARP is needed — the reply just gets forwarded hop by hop.

sections.title: What stays the same, what changes

content.body:
- **The packet never changes.** Source IP (192.168.1.1) and destination IP (192.168.4.1) stay the same for the entire journey.
- **The frame changes at every router.** Each router de-encapsulates the packet and re-encapsulates it with new source and destination MAC addresses.
- **Switches do not modify frames.** They forward them and learn MAC addresses, but never de-encapsulate or re-encapsulate.
- **ARP is only needed the first time** — after that, devices cache the neighbor MAC addresses and forward directly.

A very common exam trick: ask for the source/destination MAC or IP at a particular hop. Remember — **IP addresses are end-to-end and never change**; **MAC addresses are hop-by-hop and change at every router**. The destination MAC on a frame a PC sends to a remote host is the **default gateway's** MAC, not the remote host's.

questions.question: PC4 sends a packet to PC1 (remote network). What is the destination MAC address when the frame is sent from PC4's network interface?
questions.explanation: To reach a remote host, PC4 must first send the frame to its default gateway, R4. So the destination MAC is R4's G0/2 MAC address, FFFE.

questions.question: PC4 sends a packet to PC1. What is the source MAC address when it is received on R1's G0/0 interface?
questions.explanation: R1's G0/0 connects to R2. R2 re-encapsulated the packet using its own G0/0 MAC (CCCC) as the source, so the source MAC arriving at R1 is CCCC.

questions.question: PC4 sends a packet to PC1. What is the source MAC address when the frame is sent from SW1's G0/1 interface (toward PC1)?
questions.explanation: SW1 does not modify the frame — it simply forwards it. The frame was sent by R1 using its G0/2 MAC (AAAA) as the source, so that stays as AAAA.

questions.question: PC4 sends a packet to PC1. What is the destination IP address when it is sent from R4's G0/1 interface?
questions.explanation: Routers change the source and destination MAC addresses at each hop, but they never modify the packet itself. The destination IP stays PC1's address, 192.168.1.1.

questions.question: PC4 sends a packet to PC1. What is the source IP address when it is received on R1's G0/0 interface?
questions.explanation: The packet is not modified along the way, so the source IP address remains PC4's address, 192.168.4.1, for the entire route.
